Chapter 2: The Value of Questions and the Danger of Certainty
You know, there’s this quiet moment that sneaks up on us—maybe late at night, when the world finally calms down, or in the hush that follows a really long day. That’s when the big questions start bubbling up. Why do bad things happen to good people? What if those stories we've always believed don’t quite mean what we thought? And, is it okay to doubt, to wonder, to not have it all figured out?
For some of us, these questions feel threatening, like little cracks forming in what we thought was a solid foundation. But for others, they’re not cracks at all—they’re actually the doorway to something much deeper.
Picture this: a teenager, sitting in a youth group, listening to a lesson about faith. The leader sounds so sure, spelling out all the answers, all the rules. But this teen keeps noticing the things that don’t quite add up—the mysteries, the contradictions, the parts that just don’t fit into the lesson. There’s a real urge to ask, but also a big fear. What if asking makes them look like a troublemaker, or worse, a doubter?
And so, the questions just sit there, unspoken. Over time, that weight grows heavier. Some folks eventually walk away, thinking faith just can’t handle their doubts. Others stick around but keep their questions locked away, worried about what might happen if they finally speak up. But—and here’s the hope—there are some who find the courage to ask anyway. They risk being misunderstood, because deep down, they trust that real faith is strong enough to handle their uncertainty.
The truth is, questions aren’t the enemy of faith. Far from it. They’re actually essential. If you look at the stories in the Bible, you’ll see all kinds of people wrestling with God—arguing, doubting, even demanding answers. Abraham, Moses, David, Job... all of them brought their questions, their fears, their frustrations. Their faith wasn’t about having every answer lined up, but about being willing to keep asking, to keep seeking, and to trust that there’s always more to discover.
Most people don’t realize how easily certainty can turn into a trap. When we feel like we need to be right all the time, or defend every belief no matter what, faith can become rigid and lifeless. It’s so easy to start building walls, shutting out anything that doesn’t fit, seeing every question as a threat. But think about it—faith like that leaves no space to grow, to change, or to let the Spirit move.
There’s a story I love about a church leader who spent years preaching the same sermons, week after week, until one day the words just felt empty. The rituals lost their meaning. Then, someone in the congregation asked a question that didn’t have a neat or tidy answer. Instead of brushing it off, the leader admitted they weren’t sure either. What followed was a conversation that was honest, vulnerable, and full of life. That moment, that willingness to say “I don’t know,” became a turning point—not just for the leader, but for the entire community. Suddenly, there was room for deeper connection and real transformation.
If you take anything away from this, let it be this: faith at its best isn’t about defending a list of doctrines. It’s about staying open to mystery, to wonder, and to the possibility that there’s always more to learn. Questions aren’t a sign of weakness—they’re a sign of strength. They show that your faith is alive, that you’re willing to risk, to change, and to become something new.
